rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to span a wide retention range and reveal how many compounds elute within the window. This should give a balanced first map of retention, spacing, and whether stronger or weaker conditions are needed next.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the limiting factor is only analysis time. Shortening the gradient while keeping composition range and temperature fixed should test whether the same separation quality can be maintained with a lower time penalty and higher CRF.

The only weakness is the tight 6/7 pair in the middle of the chromatogram; reducing phi1 should make the gradient effectively shallower in that region without increasing runtime much. This may recover resolution for the critical pair while keeping all 10 peaks inside the window.

Lowering phi1 from 0.90 to 0.80 improved the critical 6/7 resolution with only a small increase in t_last, so one more step lower should test whether that pair can be fully resolved. This is a focused local optimization around an already near-optimal method.

You have already reached the maximum CRF, so the next useful experiment is to test whether a slightly shorter gradient preserves full resolution while reducing runtime further. This probes the edge of robustness around the optimal settings.

The optimum at 40 C is established, so a small temperature decrease is a sensible robustness check that may further improve selectivity for the critical 6/7 pair without changing the proven gradient shape. Since CRF is already maxed, this explores whether the method sits on a broad or narrow optimum.

Temperature reduction hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and probe phi0 instead. Raising phi0 slightly may compress the early part while redistributing the mid-gradient region around the formerly critical cluster, testing whether full resolution is robust to a modest change in starting strength.

Increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved the maximum CRF and shortened t_last slightly, so one more step higher tests whether the optimum is even more front-loaded without sacrificing the resolved mid-cluster. This is a low-risk local refinement around the current plateau of best methods.

The best region appears to be around phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.75, while lowering phi1 previously improved the critical pair. Combining the successful higher phi0 with a slightly lower phi1 should test whether selectivity in the mid-cluster can be improved further while maintaining a short run.

Methods at phi0 0.10 and 0.15 both reached the maximum CRF, so testing the lower neighboring start strength checks whether the optimum is broad on the low-phi0 side as well. This gives a useful robustness map around the already optimal condition without disturbing the proven gradient slope too much.

The max-CRF region is clearly centered at 40 C and tG 12, with phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 near 0.75; testing phi1 one step higher at the successful phi0 0.15 maps the other side of that optimum. This will define robustness in phi1 around the best method and confirm whether 0.75 is truly centered.

The current optimum is clear, so the most informative next step is an upper-side temperature robustness check complementary to the failed 35 C run. Testing 45 C will show whether 40 C is a sharp selectivity maximum or part of a broader plateau.

Both temperature deviations harmed selectivity, so stay at 40 C and test a slightly longer gradient at the other max-CRF composition. Increasing tG by one step should reveal whether there is extra robustness margin for the critical pair while likely remaining at the CRF ceiling.

The successful space is narrow in temperature but broad enough in composition that a direct comparison of phi1 0.70 at phi0 0.10 is still informative. This checks whether the slightly longer retention and stronger critical-pair resolution seen at lower phi1 can be achieved from the original best-start condition.

Since both 0.10/0.75/12 and 0.15/0.75/12 gave CRF 1.000, the remaining useful check is whether the slightly higher phi0 supports a shorter gradient better than the original method. This tests if the best composition can retain full resolution at tG 10, potentially identifying a faster robust alternative.

Since 45 C strongly affected selectivity at phi0 0.10, testing 45 C at the alternate max-CRF composition checks whether the temperature sensitivity depends on starting strength. This is a targeted robustness experiment around the best-performing composition family.

The explored optimum is well mapped around phi1 0.70–0.80, but phi1 0.85 at the successful phi0 0.10 and tG 12 has not been tested. This fills the remaining local gap on the high-phi1 side and confirms how sharply the critical 6/7 pair deteriorates as the gradient gets stronger.

The best conditions are already known, so with remaining injections the value is in finishing the local response surface. Testing phi1 0.85 at phi0 0.15 complements injection 17 and helps define whether the max-CRF plateau is centered similarly at both successful starting compositions.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical pair up to 0.70 but incurred a small time penalty; testing 0.65 will complete the low-phi1 edge and show whether resolution keeps improving enough to offset extra retention. This closes the remaining obvious gap in the composition map around the optimum.

A higher phi0 slightly shortened retention but began to hurt the critical pair, while a lower phi1 improved that pair; combining them tests whether those effects can balance. This fills a remaining untested interior point near the best region and helps map the shape of the optimum plateau.

Injection 20 found another CRF 1.000 point, suggesting the optimum extends toward higher phi0 when phi1 is lowered. Testing phi0 one step higher maps the boundary of that newly identified plateau and checks whether the early pair begins to compress too much.

Injection 20 showed the optimum extends to phi0 0.20 when phi1 is lowered to 0.70, while injection 21 located the high-phi0 failure edge. Testing phi1 0.65 at phi0 0.20 probes the low-phi1 side of this new optimum branch and maps whether extra selectivity is gained before time penalty dominates.

You now have a second CRF 1.000 point at phi0 0.20/phi1 0.70, but the high-phi1 side of that branch is still unmapped. Testing phi1 0.80 at phi0 0.20 defines the upper boundary of this plateau and clarifies whether 0.70 is uniquely favorable or part of a broader ridge.

The failure at phi0 0.25 with phi1 0.70 came from severe compression of the first pair, so testing phi1 0.75 checks whether a slightly stronger gradient can relieve that front-end crowding while keeping the mid-cluster acceptable. This is the most informative remaining boundary experiment near the newly identified high-phi0 limit.

The last unresolved question is whether lowering phi1 can rescue the front-end collapse seen at phi0 0.25 by stretching the early region enough to separate peaks 1 and 2. This final boundary test completes the high-phi0 map around the newly discovered optimum branch.
